lesson.title: Fit with least squares

lead.text: Call the bolt's true length x. Each reading is a claim about x: x = 6, x = 7 and x = 11. Written as columns, that is x times the column (1, 1, 1) on the left and the column of readings (6, 7, 11) on the right. The column of ones has three rows because there are three readings.

Now ask what a single x can produce on the left. Only multiples of (1, 1, 1), such as (3, 3, 3) or (8, 8, 8), where every entry is the same. In three-dimensional space that is a line through the origin, the span of one vector. The readings are not all equal, so they sit off that line and no value of x solves the equation.

afterFigure.text: The last lesson's idea applies here. Take the point of the line that is nearest to the readings, which is their projection onto the direction d = (1, 1, 1). The coefficient is (v · d) ÷ (d · d) = (6 + 7 + 11) ÷ 3 = 8. The nearest point is 8 copies of (1, 1, 1), so the best single value is 8 cm. That is the average of the readings, and projection shows why it is the right choice: no other value gives a point nearer to them.

lead.text: Another bolt reads 1 cm, 2 cm and 6 cm. Project the readings onto (1, 1, 1), as with the first bolt, to find the one value that fits them best.

reveal.text: You projected (1, 2, 6) onto (1, 1, 1). The coefficient is (1 + 2 + 6) ÷ 3 = 3, which is the average of the readings.

lead.text: Next, check how well 8 cm does by comparing each reading with it. The readings 6, 7 and 11 miss 8 by −2, −1 and 3. Each gap, a reading minus the fitted value, is a residual. It is the same residual as in the last lesson, the part of the readings that the fit leaves unexplained, and as a column it is (−2, −1, 3).

The residuals add up to zero. The last lesson showed that the residual of a projection is perpendicular to the direction, and here the direction is (1, 1, 1). Perpendicular means a dot product of zero, and the dot product of (−2, −1, 3) with (1, 1, 1) is just the sum of its entries. So the misses above the fit and the misses below it balance exactly.

To compare fits we need one number for the size of the misses. The plain sum cannot do it, because it cancels. So each residual is squared first and the squares are added. Squaring makes every miss positive and makes a big miss count for more. For the value 8 the total is 4 + 1 + 9 = 14. The middle reading, 7, leaves residuals −1, 0 and 4, and their squares add up to 17, which is worse.

The fit with the smallest total of squared residuals is called the least-squares fit. That total is the squared length of the residual column, and a projection is the nearest point there is. So the projection has the smallest total of all, and that is why 8 beats 7 and every other value.

steps.headline: Fit one constant to 2, 3 and 10, then total the squared residuals.

workedSteps.text: Project onto (1, 1, 1). The best constant is the average: 15 ÷ 3.
The residuals are measurement minus fit. They add up to zero.

steps.headline: Measurements 2, 4 and 9 are fitted by the constant 5. Total the squared residuals.

workedSteps.text: Square each one and add. What is the total?

lead.text: The residuals of the fit 5 to the measurements 2, 4 and 9 are −3, −1 and 4. Add them as they are, with their signs.

reveal.text: You found they cancel. The residuals of a least-squares constant are perpendicular to (1, 1, 1), so they always sum to zero.

lead.text: A single constant suits readings that should all be the same. Often a quantity changes steadily, and then a line fits better. A seedling is measured at planting, in week 0, and again in weeks 1 and 2, and stands 3 cm, 3 cm and 6 cm tall. A line c + s x describes its height after x weeks: c is the starting height and s is the slope, the number of centimetres gained each week.

Each measurement is one equation. Week 0 gives c + 0s = 3, week 1 gives c + 1s = 3 and week 2 gives c + 2s = 6. As columns, that is c times (1, 1, 1) plus s times (0, 1, 2), set equal to the heights (3, 3, 6). The first column is the one from the bolt, and the second holds the weeks. With two unknowns the left side can make every mix of the two columns, which fills a flat sheet through the origin and is wider than a single line.

afterFigure.text: The heights (3, 3, 6) do not lie on a straight line, so they are off the sheet. The method is the one from the bolt, one dimension up. The best c and s give the point of the sheet nearest to the heights, and the residuals are perpendicular to both columns. Working it through gives c = 2.5 and s = 1.5. The fitted line 2.5 + 1.5x predicts 2.5, 4 and 5.5 cm, which miss the measurements by 0.5, −1 and 0.5.

lead.text: Solving for c and s from scratch is slow, but evenly spaced measurements allow a shortcut. Take measurements at x = 0, 1 and 2, and call the residuals r₀, r₁ and r₂. Perpendicular to the column (1, 1, 1) means r₀ + r₁ + r₂ = 0. Perpendicular to the column (0, 1, 2) means r₁ + 2r₂ = 0, because the first entry is multiplied by 0. The second equation gives r₁ = −2r₂, and putting that into the first leaves r₀ = r₂.

So the first and last residuals are equal. A residual is a measurement minus the line, and the line rises by 2s between x = 0 and x = 2, so equal residuals mean that the measurements rise by exactly 2s as well. In symbols, last y − first y = 2s, which gives s = (last y − first y) ÷ 2. For the seedling this is (6 − 3) ÷ 2 = 1.5, as the figure showed.

The middle measurement plays no part in the slope. It still matters for c, because the residuals sum to zero, which makes c the average of the measurements minus s. For the seedling that is 4 − 1.5 = 2.5. The shortcut works only for measurements at x = 0, 1 and 2.
A vine is measured in weeks 0, 1 and 2 and stands 5 cm, 9 cm and 7 cm tall. Use the shortcut to find the slope of the best line c + s x.

reveal.text: You used only the first and last measurements: (7 − 5) ÷ 2 = 1. The middle one, 9, moves c and leaves the slope alone.

lead.text: A taxi's fare is £2, £5 and £8 for trips of 0, 1 and 2 km. Fit a line c + s x through these fares, where s is the cost of each extra kilometre.

lesson.orientation: Fit inconsistent measurements by minimising squared residuals.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You are measuring a metal bolt with a cheap ruler. Three readings give 6 cm, 7 cm and 11 cm. The ruler is worn at one end, so the readings disagree and no single length can match all of them.

A report still needs one number. The middle reading, 7 cm, ignores the other two. The largest, 11 cm, trusts one glance over the rest. Averaging feels fair, yet a feeling is a weak reason for choosing it.

The last lesson ended with an idea that settles this. When no exact answer exists, the best answer is the nearest one that can be reached, and that is a projection. This lesson applies it to the bolt and makes the word nearest precise. After that it fits a straight line through points that do not quite line up.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the best constant or straight line for measurements that disagree, by making the squared errors as small as possible.

recap.keyIdea: When measurements cannot all be matched, least squares picks the fit with the smallest total of squared residuals. For one constant that fit is the average, and for measurements at x = 0, 1 and 2 the slope is (last y − first y) ÷ 2.

blocks.text: Back with the bolt, you found that 8 cm is the projection of the readings onto (1, 1, 1) and that the residuals of a projection add up to zero. You then fitted a line through the seedling's heights, and used the same idea on a vine and on taxi fares.

recap.nextHook: Fitting the line took two equations solved together, because the columns (1, 1, 1) and (0, 1, 2) are not at right angles to each other. A pair at right angles would split the work in two, and the next lesson shows how to build such a pair from any two vectors.
